title: How much can I afford to discount on Black Friday 2026? (Worked examples included)
snippet: Black Friday 2026 lands on 27 November. Before you slap 30% off everything, here's how to find your real discount floor once fees, postage, ads, and returns have taken their cut. The post How much can I afford to discount on Black Friday 2026? (Worked examples included) appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Key takeaways

Black Friday is Friday 27 November 2026 and Cyber Monday is Monday 30 November 2026, although many UK retailers begin promotions earlier in November.

Your discount floor is the lowest price that still covers unit cost, fulfilment, per-order fees and a minimum profit. It’s a number, not a feeling.

Percentage fees (card, marketplace, ads) shrink as your price drops. Fixed costs (postage, packaging, per-order fees, unit cost) don’t. That’s why a 20% discount can cut your profit by 45% or more.

On a 40% gross margin, a 20% discount means you need to sell twice as many units just to make the same money.

A “was” price must represent a genuine, established usual selling price. Keep evidence of your pricing history and sales, and avoid running the lower promotional price for so long that the comparison becomes misleading.

Black Friday has a nasty habit of flattering the top line and quietly wrecking the bottom one. Orders flood in, the dashboard looks fantastic, and then January’s bank statement tells a very different story.

The reason is simple. Most small sellers set a discount by looking at what competitors are doing, or by picking a round number that “feels” generous. 

Almost nobody works out what the discount actually does to the profit on each order once card fees, marketplace commission, postage, packaging, ad spend and returns are stacked on top of the unit cost.

The goal of this article is to fix that. Read on to learn how to calculate your discount floor for your own website, for Amazon, for eBay, and for a physical shop, with real 2026 fee rates and worked examples you can copy into a spreadsheet right now (although you should always check yourself and seek the advice of experts if in any doubt; this article does not constitute legal advice.)

Here’s what we discuss:

What a discount floor is (and why percentages lie to you)

Your discount floor is the lowest price you can sell an item for and still make the minimum profit you’re prepared to accept. Below it, every extra sale costs you money.

The trap is that discounts are expressed as a percentage of the selling price, but most of your costs aren’t. 

Royal Mail charges the same £3.65 for a Tracked 48 small parcel whether the item inside sold for £45 or £27. And your  supplier does not knock 20% off the unit cost because you ran a promotion. 

So, when the price falls, the fixed costs eat a bigger and bigger share of what’s left.

That’s why the headline figure is so misleading. In the first example we quote later in this article, a 20% discount on a £45 product cuts the profit per order by 46%. A 40% discount cuts it by 91%.

Black Friday discounting step 1: Pin down your true unit cost

Unit cost is everything it takes to have one sellable item sitting on your shelf, not just the supplier invoice. When working it out, you should include:

Purchase price or materials and making time

Inbound shipping and any import duty

Packaging that goes out with the product (box, tissue, filler, label)

Any product-specific extras such as gift bags or inserts

If you make things yourself, put an honest hourly rate on your time. 

A £12 “profit” on something that took 40 minutes to make is £18 an hour before tax, and that’s before you’ve answered a single customer message.

Black Friday discounting step 2: Card and marketplace fees

These are the percentage costs, and they vary a lot by channel. Here are the current published UK rates (and bear in mind these do change, so check yourself on the sites we mention before making any big decisions):

Two things catch people out. 

First, marketplace commission is charged on the total the buyer pays, including postage. So, “free delivery” baked into the price doesn’t dodge it. 

Second, if you’re not VAT registered (and most small retail businesses aren’t until turnover passes £90,000), the 20% VAT on those fees is a real cost rather than something you reclaim. Use the VAT-inclusive rate in your sums.

Black Friday discounting step 3: Advertising

Ads get more expensive exactly when you want to run them. 

According to research from Lebesgue, the median brand’s Meta cost per mille (CPM) in the Black Friday 2025 week was 59% above its September level, and 84% higher on Black Friday itself. 

According to research from AdScale, Black Friday week CPMs were around 57% above October and cost per clicks (CPCs) around 44% higher.

The good news is that conversion rates rise too, so cost per purchase often falls. 

But you still need to budget for it. 

Take your total expected ad spend for the period, divide by the number of orders you expect, and treat that as a per-order cost. 

If you’re running Amazon Sponsored Products, use your ACoS (ad spend as a percentage of sales) as an extra percentage fee instead.

Black Friday discounting step 4: Fulfilment, packaging, and returns

Fulfilment is mostly fixed per parcel. 

Royal Mail’s online prices from 5 October 2026 start at £3.65 for Tracked 48 and £4.65 for Tracked 24. Check the online price guide for the exact price for your parcel’s size, weight and options.

Royal Mail business account customers also face a peak surcharge from 2 November 2026 to 10 January 2027, so check your rate card.

Returns are the cost almost everyone forgets, but there’s some powerful research to illuminate likely impacts and costs. 

According to the Retail Economics/ZigZag returns benchmark, UK nonfood online returns were forecast at 19.5% for 2025, with clothing the worst category at about 23.6%. According to ReBound Returns, roughly one in three shoppers send back something bought during Black Friday and Cyber Monday promotions, and returns peak in the week after. And according to EightX’s Return Rate Benchmark, each returned parcel costs a small brand roughly £10 to £25 in reverse logistics before you’ve refunded a penny.

To build this in, multiply your category’s return rate by your cost per return and add it as an expected cost per order.

The Black Friday discounting costs formula

Split your costs into two piles:

Fixed costs per order (F): Unit cost + packaging + postage + per-order fees + ad cost per order + expected returns cost

Percentage fees (P): Card or marketplace commission as a decimal, VAT included if you can’t reclaim it, plus ACoS if relevant

Then:

Discount floor price = (F + minimum profit you’ll accept) ÷ (1 − P)

Maximum discount = 1 − (floor price ÷ normal price)

Set the minimum profit to zero and you get your absolute break-even. Set it to a real number and you get a price you can actually live with.

Black Friday worked example 4: Bricks and mortar shop/high street

The catch is that rent, wages and energy are still there whatever you sell, so the real question for a shop is whether the promotion brings in enough extra footfall to cover the week’s overheads…

On a 40% margin, a 20% discount means you need to double your unit sales just to stand still. 

Ask yourself honestly whether Black Friday will do that. 

UK online revenue across the eight-day Black Friday week in 2025 was down 1.2% year on year according to Interactive Media in Retail Group (IMRG), and shoppers say they’ll spend less this year. 

The money is there. It’s just not a tidal wave.

Keep it legal: The “was” price test

A discount is only a discount if the higher price was real. 

The current Advertising Standards Authority (ASA)/Committee of Advertising Practice (CAP) guidance says the reference price should represent a genuine, established usual selling price. The ASA has upheld rulings this year against major retailers whose “was” prices hadn’t been charged for long enough or in sufficient volume, and it could expect detailed day-by-day pricing and sales data covering at least three months to back up any savings claim. 

The High Court’s July 2026 ruling in the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) Emma Sleep case rejected a rigid 1:2 sales ratio, but the duration test survived: the product should have been on sale at the “was” price for at least as long as it’s offered at the discount.

Practically, that means if your sale runs 23 November to 1 December, the full price needs to have been live from mid-November at the very latest, and ideally for a month or more. 

Export your price history for your top lines now, and drop the strikethrough on anything that doesn’t qualify.

Final thoughts

Black Friday rewards sellers who know their numbers, not sellers who shout the biggest percentage. 

Once you’ve separated your fixed per-order costs from your percentage fees, the discount floor is easily calculated via a one-line formula, and you can set a headline that’s generous to customers without being reckless with your margin.

The pattern across all four examples we quote above is consistent. Online sellers with postage and marketplace fees usually hit zero profit somewhere between 35% and 47% off, and a sensible floor with real profit left in sits around 20% to 30%. Physical shops have more room per item but need the footfall to cover overheads. Fashion sellers need to price in returns before they price in anything else.

Three things to do this week: 

Calculate your floor for every line you plan to promote.

Check your “was” prices will stand up.

Decide in advance how many extra orders you need before the discount pays for itself. 

If the maths doesn’t work, a smaller discount, a bundle, or free delivery over a threshold will often do more for you than a headline number you can’t afford.

FAQs about Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales

			

			

	

What’s a safe Black Friday discount for a small online business?

	

			

There’s no universal figure, but once postage, marketplace fees and ad costs are included, the examples above suggest most small online sellers find their break-even sits between roughly 35% and 47% off, and a floor that keeps meaningful profit is usually 20% to 30%. Run the formula for each product rather than applying one percentage across the range.

	

	

How do I calculate my discount floor?

	

			

Add up your fixed costs per order (unit cost, packaging, postage, per-order fees, ad spend per order, expected returns cost) plus the minimum profit you want. Divide by one minus your percentage fees. The result is your floor price. Compare it with your normal price to get the maximum discount.

	

	

Do marketplace fees go down when I discount?

	

			

Yes, because they’re a percentage of the sale, but they don’t fall as fast as your profit does. Postage, packaging and unit cost stay exactly the same, so they take up a bigger share of a smaller price.

	

	

Should I include VAT on fees in my calculation?

	

			

If you’re not VAT registered, yes. Amazon, eBay and Etsy all add 20% VAT to their fees, and you can’t reclaim it. A 15% Amazon referral fee is about 18.4% in cash once the digital services fee and VAT are added. If you are VAT registered, use the ex-VAT rate.

	

	

Can I show a “was”/“previously sold at” price on Black Friday?

	

			

Only if the higher price was genuine and represented the product’s established usual selling price. Keep pricing and sales records to support the claim. Factors such as how recently and for how long the higher price applied, and whether meaningful sales were made at that price, may all be relevant. The ASA has upheld complaints where the promotional price lasted longer than the supposed reference price.

	

	

How much should I budget for returns?

	

			

Use your category’s return rate multiplied by your cost per return. Across UK non-food online retail as a whole, the forecast return rate was around 19.5% in 2025, rising to about 23.6% for clothing.

title: Autumn Budget 2026: What it means for your business
snippet: Here are the announcements that affect sole traders, small, and medium-sized businesses—plus what it all means in practice, and the next steps to take. The post Autumn Budget 2026: What it means for your business appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
The UK Chancellor delivered the Autumn Budget 2026 on Wednesday 28 October, and it had more in it for businesses than many expected.

A long list of targeted measures touches almost every part of running a company: business rates, minimum wage, mileage, capital allowances, online selling, e-invoicing and even how you’ll be expected to pay HMRC in future.

Below is a summary of what was announced, grouped by area, with the figures and start dates you need. Most changes take effect from April 2027 onwards, and some not until 2029, so there’s time to plan. 

Here’s what we discuss:

Business bills, including rates

Headline news for the Budget was the likely abolition of the standing charge on home gas bills at some point in 2027, with the Chancellor charging Ofgem with implementation.  What’s more, homes classed in Council Tax bands A to D will get a £100 energy payment.

Alas, none of this is extended to energy bills for businesses. Standing charges have never been capped in the same way, and can vary enormously depending on the size of the enterprise and the nature of supply contract. 

Don’t forget previously-announced measures, though. From April 2027, around 10,000 energy-intensive manufacturers in eligible sectors will see electricity bills cut by up to 25% under the British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme, which exempts them from the indirect costs of the Renewables Obligation, Feed-in Tariffs and Capacity Market. Note that inclusion in this isn’t automatic. Eligibility depends on SIC and HS codes and a minimum electricity intensity, and the application window ends on 30 November 2026.

When it comes to business rates, it’s once again retail, hospitality and leisure (RHL) businesses that benefit. From April 2027, qualifying pubs, social clubs and most live music venues will receive an additional 20 percentage points of relief, bringing their total relief to 35%. The Chancellor has also increased the Small Business Rates Relief thresholds for qualifying RHL properties in England. From 1 April 2027, properties with a rateable value of up to £18,000 will qualify for 100% relief, with relief tapering to zero for properties with a rateable value between £18,000 and £21,000. Previously, these thresholds were £12,000 and £15,000 respectively. The government estimates that the changes will mean 70,000 more businesses pay no business rates.

What this means for businesses

Check your rateable value on the Valuation Office Agency website and challenge it if you believe it is incorrect. The government offers a service to calculate rates.

With no changes in the budget affecting bills, it’s once again down to businesses to get the best deals for their utility usage. Businesses with high energy usage should consider using third-party intermediaries (TPis; aka brokers), while other businesses should use price comparison sites.

After all, every utility, software, and telecoms bill you pay is the product of a decision made at some point. The quickest win is to find out when each of those decisions is next up for grabs, and then ensure bill contract management is a clearly-identified part of someone’s job. They should put every contract end date and notice window in one shared calendar, with a reminder 90 days out. 

Never, ever end up using out-of-contract rates. These can easily be up to 50% higher than a fixed deal. You can usually switch with as little as 28 days notice, so do so, especially if you “inherited” the utility provider when you moved into your premises.

Finally, read the small print on how prices can move during the term. This kind of effort up front pays dividends in the long-run. Mid-contract price rises are an old trick, even if you’re on an introductory deal, and if they match the rate of inflation with a little extra added-on then it can be a substantial increase. 

Corporation tax and VAT

The main rate of Corporation Tax stays at 25%, and the small profits rate at 19%, for the financial year starting 1 April 2028. As was previously announced, marginal relief for profits between £50,000 and £250,000 continues unchanged.

The rates of VAT and the £90,000 registration threshold haven’t changed in this Budget, either. 

But there are some interesting VAT developments elsewhere. 

The headline measure affects online sellers. From October 2027, marketplaces will be responsible for collecting VAT on sales by UK VAT-registered businesses, and by any other UK business with annual sales of £90,000 or more on a single platform. Note that this applies per platform, and not across all marketplaces combined, and only covers goods located in the UK at the point of sale to consumers.

What’s more, personal sales, second-hand goods, and business-to-business transactions are excluded.

The government also announced that how VAT is paid is also changing: From April 2029, businesses will need a Direct Debit instruction in place for VAT return liabilities, if they don’t have one already, with other payment methods still allowed before a cut-off date. This matches a similar announcement for PAYE. 

And finally, there’s a change if you use services overseas. From April 2027, if your business isn’t VAT registered and you buy services from overseas suppliers, those suppliers will charge you UK VAT directly rather than the reverse charge applying.

The customs treatment of low-value imports is being reformed, with implementation now due by October 2028, six months earlier than previously announced. 

What this means for businesses

If you sell through a marketplace, and have been casting a blind eye to your VAT liability, then the game is over. You can expect the marketplaces you use to contact you. If you’re not VAT registered then now’s the time to do so. 

If you pay VAT in any other way than via Direct Debit, then you’ve over a year to sort it out. 

The low-value import changes bring small parcels closer to the treatment of goods imported as freight, so overseas sellers can’t undercut UK businesses by sidestepping duty. Alongside the marketplace VAT change, it narrows the pricing advantage some overseas sellers currently enjoy, which is good news if you compete with them.

Income tax, National Insurance, and wages

Headline rates of Income Tax and National Insurance contributions (NICs) are unchanged.

This means no change to the government continued freeze of Income Tax thresholds for employees and the self-employed in England and Northern Ireland until 2030/31.

However, Class 2 NICs Small Profits Threshold rises to £7,355 for 2027-28, and the voluntary Class 2 rate becomes £3.80 a week. 

Note that the Scotland and Welsh parliaments have their own rules: the Welsh budget is due on 17 November 2026, and the Scottish budget is due on 3 December 2026. 

As expected, National Minimum Wage (NMW) and National Living Wage (NLW) hourly rates will rise by 3.9% as of 1 April 2027, as follows (according to the usual age brackets):

National Living Wage (21 and over): Rises from £12.71 to £13.21 per hour

National Minimum Wage (18 to 20): Rises from £10.85 to £11.27 per hour

National Minimum Wage (16 to 17): Rises from £8.00 to £8.31 per hour

Apprentice rate: Rises from £8.00 to £8.31 per hour

The Lower Earnings Limit for Class 1 National Insurance rises to £6,916 a year (£133 a week) for 2027-28, uprated by September’s 3.5% CPI figure. It’s the point at which employees start building entitlement to statutory payments and the State Pension, so update payroll settings before April 2027.

If you’re self employed and pay your Income Tax on account twice each year, how you pay will change as of April 2029. Details are due in yet-to-be-announced legislation, but there will also be an option to pay more frequently via PAYE (that is, paying any outside Income Tax liability via your existing salary payments, if you’re employed by a business). 

If you’re running a side hustle or other micro business, perhaps as a hobby, there’s some good news: The trading allowance rises from £1,000, to £3,000. This means that you don’t need to pay tax on income up to that amount, or even tell HMRC (although other income or reporting requirements may still apply).

Separately, employers will have to report and tax most benefits in kind through payroll rather than on P11Ds: company cars and vans, fuel and medical benefits from 6 April 2027, and almost all other benefits from 6 April 2028.

What this means for businesses

As always, there’s a need to avoid the hidden tripwires in pay runs. A rise in NMW and NLW narrows your margin for error. Deductions for uniforms or tools, unpaid pre-shift briefings, travel between jobs, salary sacrifice schemes, and apprentices still on the apprentice rate after their first year can all drag pay below the legal minimum without anyone noticing. 

And that’s bad. Penalties imposed by HMRC can reach 200% of the underpayment, capped at £20,000 per worker.

A rise in the National Living Wage pushes up every number built on top of it including employer National Insurance, pension contributions, holiday pay, and overtime premiums. If you’re going to model the rises across the year, or model for new hires, then ensure you model the fully loaded hour, not just the hourly rate.

So-called fiscal drag remains an issue for many employees, who see annual increases in income via wage rises move them into higher tax brackets, meaning proportionately less of that increase than they might anticipate arrives in their pockets. Disappointment about this can unfortunately be directed to your business, despite the fact it’s beyond your control. However, it can be offset to a greater or lesser degree by looking at non-cash benefits-in-kind to create attractive employment packages.

Making Tax Digital

The expansion of Making Tax Digital for Income Tax goes ahead as planned in April 2027, with sole traders and landlords with qualifying income over £30,000 joining the scheme.

The Budget somewhat unexpectedly extended the ‘soft landing period‘, which is the period of grace whereby missed quarterly update deadlines were not penalised by HMRC across 2026/27. Anyone required to join in April 2027 won’t receive late submission penalty points for their 2027-28 quarterly updates. The updates still have to be sent, though, because you can’t file your tax return until they’re in.

It was also announced that a few groups are exempt from MTD until further notice, including those eligible for qualifying care relief, non-UK resident foreign entertainers and sportspeople, and expected non-residents.

What this means for businesses

If you’re part of the April 2027 MTD intake, start preparing now. There’s never been a better time to start keeping digital records.

Then use the penalty-free first year to get your software and quarterly routine working properly, rather than treating it as a reason to delay.

Fuel, vehicles, travel, and haulage

Fuel duty has been frozen again, for the 16th year in a row. What’s more, the 5p cut—announced way back in 2022 as a supposedly temporary cost-of-living measure—is extended from 1 January 2027 to 30 June 2027. At that point, rates are set to return to pre-2022 levels and will rise with RPI from 1 July 2027.

Both measures are undoubtedly welcome but neither will alter the cost of fuel, of course.

For those that use their own vehicles for work activities—so called grey fleet drivers—the 55p rate in the approved mileage allowance payment (AMAP) rates for the first 10,000 miles, introduced in May 2026 and backdated to 6 April 2026, is now permanent. 

From 6 April 2027 the rate for miles above 10,000 also rises, from 25p to 35p.

Mileage Allowance Relief (MAR) and Relevant Motoring Expenditure (RME) changes to accommodate and match AMAP are also now permanent.

AMAP is the maximum rate that can be claimed by employees for personal vehicle use, and is reimbursed free of tax and National Insurance by employers through wages, with there being no requirement for employee or employer to report it to HMRC provided the rate is at or below the AMAP rates (although detailed records still need to be kept).

Sole traders can deduct AMAP rates as a simplified expense on their tax return.

The rates are now as follows, and claims can be backdated to April 2026:

Cars and vans: 55p/mile for the first 10,000 miles, then 35p/mile for miles driven above 10,000

Motorcycles: 24p/mile, regardless of miles covered

Bicycles: 20p/mile, regardless of miles covered

There’s also a potential extra 5p per mile if transporting fellow employees for business.

On the flip side, if you provide staff with company vans they can use privately, or pay for private fuel in company cars or vans, the taxable benefit figures rise in line with inflation from 6 April 2027. The flat-rate van benefit charge goes up to £4,310 (from £4,170), the van fuel benefit charge to £825 (from £798) and the car fuel benefit multiplier to £30,200 (from £29,200).

And finally, some business travel-related changes: From 6 April 2028, the benchmark scale rates employers can pay for staff meals on business trips, without checking receipts, rise to £20 for journeys over 5 hours, £60 over 10 hours and £75 over 24 hours. The 200-plus overseas rates will be replaced by a simpler tiered system linked to these.

What this means for businesses

If an employee’s private fuel use is modest, the tax on the fuel benefit can cost more than the fuel itself, so it may be cheaper for both sides to have them repay private mileage instead. Note these benefits must be payrolled through RTI from 6 April 2027 under the new mandatory rules.

If you pay below the AMAP rate, you’re leaving your staff out of pocket twice. They absorb the shortfall, and most won’t know they can claim Mileage Allowance Relief on the difference. Paying the full rate costs you nothing extra in tax or National Insurance, so unless there’s a good reason not to, pay it. 

Also check your expenses system records business mileage per trip with dates and destinations, because HMRC’s position is that an unsupported mileage claim is taxable pay, and the mandatory payrolling of benefits from April 2027 means payroll data will be scrutinised more closely.

Benchmark scale rates are a quiet admin win. From April 2028, you can pay £20, £60 or £75 for meals on qualifying trips with no receipts to collect or check. If you’re still processing individual lunch receipts for travelling staff, moving to scale rates removes a layer of paperwork for your finance team and gives employees certainty about what they’ll get back. You’ll still need a record that the trip happened and how long it lasted, but not what was eaten.

E-invoicing

The Budget confirmed the timetable for the preliminary steps for mandatory e-invoicing. From 1 April 2029, VAT-registered businesses will need to be able to issue and receive structured electronic invoices for domestic transactions where a VAT invoice is required, unless exempt.

That means invoices in a machine-readable format exchanged system to system, not a PDF attached to an email. There’s a single start date rather than staged cohorts, and Peppol, the international framework already used widely in Europe and Australasia, will be the UK’s core interoperability standard.

Much of the detail is still to come, and we’ll be covering it in detail here on Sage Advice. HMRC plans to consult on technical standards in spring 2027, publish practical guidance in autumn 2027, and finalise scope, exemptions, standards, business identifiers and provider requirements between October 2027 and April 2028. 

Existing legacy arrangements will be allowed to continue, provided businesses using them can also exchange compliant e-invoices through the UK framework.

Note: The 2029 mandate doesn’t introduce routine reporting of invoice data to HMRC. A separate consultation on the possible future use of e-invoice data runs until 20 January 2027, and no reporting duty has been decided.

What this means for businesses

Two and a half years sounds like a long time, but it’s roughly two average software upgrade cycles, so this is a planning item rather than a panic item. 

The first practical step is to ask your accounting or invoicing software provider, in writing, whether they intend to support Peppol e-invoicing and when. Most mainstream packages are expected to build it in, but you want that confirmed before your next renewal, not after.

Think about receiving as well as sending. The requirement covers both directions, and for many small businesses the bigger change will be how supplier invoices arrive and get matched to purchase orders and payments. If your bookkeeping still relies on someone keying in figures from PDFs, e-invoicing is the point at which that stops being necessary, and it’s worth tidying up your supplier records and payment processes in the meantime so you benefit from the automation.

If you sell to larger customers or the public sector, expect them to move early. Big organisations will want all their suppliers on structured invoicing well before the deadline, so being e-invoice ready could become a condition of winning or keeping contracts from 2028 onwards. 

Investment and entrepreneurship

A new Founders’ Relief will apply a 10% rate of Capital Gains Tax to qualifying disposals of shares, up to a lifetime limit of £10 million of gains per individual, for disposals made on or after 6 April 2027. It’s aimed at founders and significant early investors in high-growth, innovative UK companies, although the government is still working out some of the details—so ensure you monitor the situation.

Under the proposed conditions, you’d need to have held 25% of the ordinary share capital when the company’s trade (or preparation for it) began, held the shares for at least five years, and been UK resident for at least five continuous tax years.

Less welcome news is that the lifetime limit for Business Asset Disposal Relief (BADR) halves from £1 million to £500,000 for qualifying disposals on or after 6 April 2027, with transitional rules for contracts signed but not completed before that date. The Chancellor said this means no change for three in four claimants.

On investment, the main rate first-year allowance rises from 40% to 50% for spending from 1 January 2027, while the main writing-down allowance falls to 12% from April 2027. Minor fixes to SEIS, EIS and VCT rules follow from 6 April 2027. Note that the 50% allowance does not apply to all expenditure and that eligible assets already qualifying for full expensing are treated differently.

What this means for business

If you’re planning to sell your business, the BADR change is the one to act on. 

Gains above £500,000 will lose the lower rate from April 2027, so anyone with a sale already in motion should speak to their accountant about timing and whether the transitional provisions apply. For most owner-managers selling for less than that, nothing changes.

Founders’ Relief is more specific. The 25% founding stake, five-year holding period, and the proposed “sustained high growth” test mean it’s for scale-ups, and not the typical small business.

The allowance change rewards investing sooner. From January 2027, up to half the cost of qualifying plant and machinery can be deducted in year one, for assets that don’t qualify for full expensing, so if you’re weighing up equipment purchases, the maths tilts towards early 2027 rather than late 2026.

Final thoughs

This was a Budget of many small changes rather than one big one, and that works in your favour. Nothing lands before April 2027, and the biggest shifts, in e-invoicing and how you pay HMRC, are two years or more away. 

Use that time well. 

Pick the three or four measures that apply to you, put the dates in your calendar, run the numbers, and talk to your accountant before the year-end rush.

title: Freelancer tax terms explained in plain English
snippet: Self Assessment, taxable profit, and payments on account are easier to understand when you know which part of the freelance tax process each term describes. The post Freelancer tax terms explained in plain English appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Key takeaways

Freelancer describes how you work. Self-employed describes working for yourself, while sole trader is the business structure many freelancers use. 

Turnover is business income before costs. Profit is what remains after costs, while taxable profit reflects allowable expenses and any relevant adjustments. 

Self Assessment is the tax-reporting system. A tax return is the submission you make through that system. 

Making Tax Digital quarterly updates are cumulative summaries, not extra tax returns, and they do not make Income Tax payable four times a year. 

Payments on account are advance payments towards a future bill, which is why a first January payment can be larger than expected. 

Search for an answer to a freelance tax question and you might get a barrage of unfamiliar terms. You want to know whether software is tax deductible, but the answer discusses allowable expenses and taxable profit. You check a deadline and find Self Assessment, payments on account and balancing payments. 

There’s no need to learn the whole tax system. Most of its vocabulary answers one of four questions: 

How are you working? 

Which money counts when tax is calculated? 

What must you record and report? 

What might you need to pay, and when? 

Once you know which question a term answers, it becomes easier to read HMRC guidance, understand what software is showing you and ask an accountant a precise question. 

This article focuses on UK self-employed sole traders. Partnerships and limited companies have different legal and tax rules. It provides general information rather than personal tax or accounting advice. 

Terms that describe how you work

Let’s start our glossary with some of the basic tax terminology that covers you, and what you do.

Freelance work and sole trader status 

Freelancer describes a way of working rather than a legal structure. A freelancer normally provides services to different clients or works on a series of projects instead of being permanently employed by one organisation. 

Self-employed generally means that you work for yourself and take responsibility for the business, rather than having tax deducted from those earnings through PAYE. Employment status depends on the real working arrangement, not simply the label in a contract. 

Sole trader is a business structure used by many freelancers. You run the business as an individual and are not legally separate from it. You can still use a trading name, collaborate with other freelancers or employ people; “sole” refers to ownership. 

A small amount of freelance income does not always mean you must file a tax return. The trading allowance and your wider circumstances can affect the position, so check HMRC’s current Self Assessment filing conditions. In the November 2026 budget, the trading allowance was boosted from £1000 to £3000. 

Terms that describe your money 

Now, let’s move on to the thing that makes the world go around, whether we like it or not—plus, how it relates to you, and what you do.

From turnover to taxable profit 

Turnover is the total business income generated before business expenses are deducted. You may also see it called gross income, gross trading income or gross receipts. If £35,000 came from client work and £2,000 from licensing, turnover would be £37,000 before costs. 

Profit is broadly what remains after business costs. A freelancer can have a busy year with strong sales but much less profit after paying for collaborators, software, travel, insurance and other costs. Turnover therefore cannot tell you what is available to spend personally. 

Taxable profit is the profit figure used in the tax calculation after allowable expenses and any required adjustments. In a simple example, £30,000 of turnover minus £5,000 of allowable expenses could produce taxable profit of £25,000. Real calculations may involve other rules. 

How allowable expenses work 

Allowable expenses are qualifying business costs deducted when taxable profit is worked out. Depending on the circumstances, they might include software, insurance, accountancy fees, advertising, office supplies, business travel or some working-from-home costs. Mixed personal and business use can change what qualifies. See HMRC’s guidance on expenses if you’re self-employed. 

An allowable expense can reduce taxable profit; it does not normally mean HMRC refunds the full purchase price. The cost still leaves the business account, which is why tax treatment and cash flow are related but different. 

How the Personal Allowance works 

The Personal Allowance is the amount of income an individual can generally receive before paying Income Tax. It applies across relevant personal income rather than separately to every job. If you are employed and freelance on the side, your salary may already use some or all of it. Check the current Income Tax rates and allowances. 

Terms connected with recording and reporting 

When you make money from your work, you need to tell HMRC. Here’s a glossary of the terms required.

The tax year and Self Assessment 

The UK tax year for individuals runs from 6 April to 5 April. The accounting method you use can affect when income and expenses are recorded, so money received close to the start or end of April may need particular attention. 

Self Assessment is the system used to report income and other relevant information to HMRC when tax has not already been dealt with automatically.  

A tax return is the form or digital submission made through that system. “Return” does not mean you will receive money back; the calculation may show tax to pay, nothing further due or an overpayment. 

What records to keep 

Record keeping means maintaining accurate information and evidence about business income and expenses. This can include invoices, payments, receipts, bank statements and evidence supporting business costs. You do not normally send every receipt with the return, but you need records that support the figures. HMRC explains which records self-employed people should keep. 

Making Tax Digital (MTD) and quarterly updates 

Making Tax Digital (MTD) for Income Tax requires affected sole traders and landlords to keep digital records, use compatible software, send quarterly updates and submit their annual tax return through that software. Under the current rollout, it applies from April 2026 where qualifying income is over £50,000, from April 2027 over £30,000 and from April 2028 over £20,000. Qualifying income is gross self-employment and property income before expenses. Check HMRC’s current MTD guidance. 

A quarterly update is a cumulative summary of income and expenses from the start of the tax year to the end of the update period. It is not another complete tax return and does not move Income Tax payments to a quarterly timetable. HMRC’s quarterly update guidance explains what each update contains. 

Terms connected with paying 

So, once you’ve made the money, and told HMRC, you’ll need to pay your taxes.

Income Tax and National Insurance 

Income Tax is charged on taxable income above available allowances. For a sole trader, taxable business profit contributes to that calculation alongside other relevant income. The calculation is based on the wider personal tax position, not separately on each freelance invoice. 

National Insurance is separate from Income Tax, although a self-employed person may deal with both through Self Assessment. Class 4 contributions depend on profits above the applicable threshold. Class 2 contributions are treated as paid when profits reach the specified level, while some people with lower profits may pay voluntarily to protect their record. Check current self-employed National Insurance rules. 

Tax bills and advance payments 

A tax bill can include Income Tax, Class 4 National Insurance, a balancing payment for the year reported and a payment on account towards the next one. Payments on account are normally paid on 31 January and 31 July. Each is usually half the relevant tax owed for the previous year. 

Payments on account are generally not required if the previous Self Assessment bill was below £1,000 or more than 80% of the tax was collected outside Self Assessment. When they first apply, January can include the full bill just reported plus the first advance payment for the next year. 

A balancing payment is the difference due when earlier payments on account do not cover the final bill. Paying too much may instead produce a refund or credit. 

Note that, in the 2026 Autumn Budget, there was talk of changing how sole trader tax payments are made, so you might want to keep an eye on this. In particular, you may also be possible be able to pay taxes on your freelance work through any salaried work you do for an employer, which should make life a lot more straightforward.

Final thoughts: How the terms fit together 

Imagine Maya is a self-employed illustrator and sole trader. She records income and costs, so turnover shows money generated and allowable expenses help determine taxable profit. She submits a tax return through Self Assessment. 

The calculation considers allowances, Income Tax and National Insurance; her statement shows any balancing payment or payments on account. Understanding the terms shows which step each figure belongs to. 

Tax rules, thresholds and individual circumstances vary. Check current GOV.UK guidance or speak to a qualified adviser if you are unsure how a term applies to you. 

Frequently asked questions 

			

			

	

Can a freelancer also be a sole trader? 

	

			

Freelancer describes a way of working. Self-employed generally means working for yourself and taking responsibility for the business. Sole trader is the business structure many self-employed freelancers use. The same person can therefore be described by all three terms, but they do not mean exactly the same thing. 

	

	

Is turnover the same as profit? 

	

			

No. Turnover is business income before costs are deducted. Profit is broadly what remains after business costs. Taxable profit is the figure used for the tax calculation after allowable expenses and any required adjustments. A strong turnover figure can therefore sit alongside a much smaller profit. 

	

	

Is Self Assessment the same as a tax return? 

	

			

No. Self Assessment is the overall system for reporting relevant income and calculating what is due. The tax return is the specific form or digital submission made through that system. The phrases are often used interchangeably, but the distinction explains why one system can cover several types of income. 

	

	

Do MTD quarterly updates mean quarterly tax payments? 

	

			

No. The updates are cumulative summaries of income and expenses sent through compatible software. Affected people still submit one annual tax return and pay their tax bill on the existing timetable. Payments on account may fall in January and July, but they are not created by quarterly updates. 

	

	

Why can a first January Self Assessment payment be higher than expected? 

	

			

When payments on account first apply, the January amount can include the full tax bill for the year just reported and the first advance payment towards the next year. The second advance payment is normally due in July. Check the statement rather than assuming the whole January amount relates to one tax year.

title: How to manage feast-or-famine income as a freelancer
snippet: A busy month can bring financial relief, but it doesn’t tell you what you can afford next month. Here’s how to plan around uneven freelance income, build a buffer and make payments more predictable. The post How to manage feast-or-famine income as a freelancer appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Key takeaways

Plan around essential costs and a cautious income estimate, rather than your strongest month. 

Forecast when payments should arrive, not just when you expect to finish the work. 

Use stronger months to cover future gaps, while keeping tax money separate. 

Agree deposits, staged payments or recurring work where they suit the project. 

Set aside regular time to find your next commission, even when you’re busy. 

You finish a big project, send the invoice and finally get paid. For a moment, the money worries ease. 

Then you look at next month’s diary. A client hasn’t confirmed their brief. Another project has moved back. Your rent, software subscriptions and household bills will arrive as usual. 

Feast-or-famine income is the cycle of strong earnings followed by leaner periods. For creative freelancers, it can come from project work, seasonal demand or clients paying at different times. Sometimes you have plenty of work but little cash because the payment comes later. 

Not every freelancer accepts feast-or-famine as inevitable.  

Writing in Freelancer Magazine, copywriter Anita Ellis says she has experienced just one short “famine” in five years of freelancing. Her approach includes continuing to market her business even when work is plentiful. 

Managing your business means knowing what must be covered, when money is likely to arrive and how much of a stronger month needs to last. This guide is written for UK freelancers operating as sole traders, and here’s what we discuss:

Work out what you need each month 

Start with two figures: the essential cost of running your business and the amount you need to contribute to your household. 

Business costs might include software, insurance, workspace and equipment repayments. Your personal baseline could include housing, food, utilities, travel and minimum debt repayments. 

Account for bills that don’t arrive monthly, too. An annual subscription still needs funding, even if the payment isn’t due this week. Keep business and household costs distinct so you can see where the pressure comes from.  

Next, review the money you’ve actually received over the past six to twelve months, if you have that history. Notice lower-income periods, seasonal patterns and dependence on particular clients.  

MoneyHelper’s guidance on irregular income recommends budgeting around your lowest monthly income. That gives you a cautious starting point. 

But if some months bring no payments at all, you’ll need to plan across several months and identify how savings or payments from stronger periods can bridge the gaps. 

An average helps you understand the overall pattern. It cannot guarantee that money will be available when a bill falls due. 

If your income repeatedly falls short of essential costs, budgeting alone won’t close the gap. You may need to review your rates, costs, client mix or other sources of income. 

Forecast money arriving, not just work booked 

A £3,000 commission is encouraging. Yet if you finish it next month, invoice afterwards and then wait for payment, it won’t necessarily cover this month’s bills. 

At the SMB Advisory Board convened by Sage, a business owner described how customers’ 30- or 60-day payment terms, alongside different reporting deadlines, made it harder to maintain an overview of their finances. 

Build a simple forecast for the next three months. Record your available opening balance, expected payments, business costs and planned transfers for household spending. Keep existing tax reserves outside the amount you treat as available, and allow for further money you need to set aside. 

Separate incoming money into three groups: 

Invoiced work: The amount due and expected payment date. 

Confirmed work not yet invoiced: Agreed projects, including when you can invoice and when payment is expected. 

Possible work: Enquiries and proposals that haven’t been agreed. 

Count each payment once. When you invoice confirmed work, move it into the invoiced group rather than adding it again. 

Build your main plan around invoiced and confirmed work, recognising that even these payments can slip. Keep possible commissions in a separate scenario. 

Then test a delay. What happens if your largest payment arrives a month late? Where does the first shortfall appear? 

That tells you when to follow up, discuss payment stages or reconsider a commitment. Update the forecast each week when project or payment dates change. 

Track tax payment dates alongside it and check that your separate reserve will cover them. If a tax payment is fully funded from a reserve you’ve already excluded, don’t deduct it again from your available balance. 

Give a good month a job 

When several client payments arrive together, decide what the money needs to cover before increasing your spending. 

Allow for tax and other obligations, upcoming business costs and your household contribution. Then consider what can go towards future quieter periods. 

Check your tax payment dates as well as the amount you’re reserving. If Self Assessment payments on account apply to you, they are normally due on 31 January and 31 July and are usually based on the previous year’s tax. Payments based on a stronger year can therefore fall due during a quieter period. 

If you expect to owe less tax, you can apply to reduce them, but reducing them too far can lead to interest on the shortfall. 

Rather than transferring whatever arrives straight into your personal account, you could aim for a more consistent monthly transfer. For a sole trader, this is a budgeting habit; it doesn’t turn the transfer into an employee salary. 

Here’s a simplified example, starting with no buffer. The available income shown is what remains after business costs and tax reserves have been allowed for. 

Month

January’s stronger income supports the next two months. But by the end of March, the buffer is gone. The pattern only works for longer if later income replenishes it. 

Choose a transfer your forecast can support, and review it when circumstances change. 

If you can’t build a large reserve immediately, start with a smaller target: one essential bill, then a week of costs. Keep the quiet-period buffer separate from tax money so you can see what is available. 

Make the payment pattern more predictable 

You may not control when a client commissions work, but you can discuss how they pay for it. 

For a longer project, agree a deposit or payments at defined milestones. Set out the scope, amounts, invoice dates and payment terms before work starts. 

For clients with an ongoing need, a monthly arrangement might suit both sides. 

In the 2022 Money Diary of an entrepreneurial accountant, the business owner explains that most of their clients paid their annual fees in fixed monthly instalments, collected automatically by direct debit. They describe this as helping cash flow for both sides and reducing payment admin. 

For a creative freelancer, the comparable opportunity might be a defined monthly package of design, writing or editing. 

Be specific about deliverables, revisions, availability and cancellation terms. A monthly fee needs boundaries so it doesn’t become an open-ended workload. 

Regular income also needs to be weighed against fixed costs. In another 2022 Money Diary, a beauty studio owner describes the pressure after moving to premises where her rent more than doubled, while finding additional renters proved harder than expected. 

These individual experiences illustrate two decisions worth making deliberately: how you collect income and which recurring costs you take on. 

Before adding a subscription, workspace or equipment repayment, check whether you could still cover it during a weaker period. 

Protect time for the next commission 

When you’re busy delivering, finding future work can slip down the list. The risk is finishing the current project with nothing ready to follow it. 

Reserve a small, repeatable block for business development during busy weeks. Follow up a proposal, contact a previous client or share a relevant piece of work. Choose actions that fit the clients you want. 

Ellis describes marketing as something to keep doing “especially when you’re experiencing a ‘feast’” 

Look at how far ahead your confirmed work extends. Also check whether one client accounts for most of your expected income. 

More clients can spread risk, but they bring more admin, and several clients may still depend on the same seasonal budgets. Aim for a manageable mix of projects and ongoing work. 

Being booked solid isn’t the whole measure of a healthy freelance business. The work needs to leave enough money and time to support what comes next. 

Final thoughts: Plan what your next payment needs to cover 

Start this week with your essential monthly costs and a three-month payment forecast. Then decide what the next strong payment needs to cover before it arrives. 

FAQs about uneven freelance income 

			

			

	

How do I budget when I don’t know what I’ll earn? 

	

			

Start with essential costs, available money and payments from agreed work. Keep potential commissions separate. Update the forecast as work is confirmed, and test what happens if a payment is delayed. 

	

	

Should I pay myself the same amount every month? 

	

			

It can help, if your income and buffer support it. Review the amount regularly. If it keeps draining your reserves, adjust the transfer or address the underlying income gap. 

	

	

How much should I save for quiet months? 

	

			

Base your target on essential costs, likely gaps between payments and how dependent you are on particular clients. Start with an achievable amount and build from there. Keep this reserve separate from money set aside for tax. 

	

	

Will a retainer solve feast-or-famine income? 

	

			

Not on its own. It can make part of your income more predictable where a client needs ongoing work, but it won’t guarantee renewals or timely payment. Agree the scope, workload, payment terms and notice period, and consider how you would manage if it ended. 

	

	

What if I’m busy but still short of money? 

	

			

Look at timing first: the gap between doing the work, invoicing and receiving payment. Then review project costs and the time you spend on delivery, revisions and admin. The problem may be payment timing, low margins or both.

title: Allowable expenses for creative freelancers: What can you claim?
snippet: Software, studio hire, a new laptop, or coffee while you work: which costs count as business expenses? Here’s how to separate claimable costs from personal spending and keep useful records. The post Allowable expenses for creative freelancers: What can you claim? appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Key takeaways

Allowable expenses reduce taxable profit; they don’t make a purchase free. 

The purpose of a purchase matters more than which account you pay from. 

For costs with separable business and personal use, claim only the business share. 

Everyday clothing, ordinary meals and client entertaining are generally not allowable. 

Keep evidence and check uncertain costs before including them in your claim. 

A design subscription feels straightforward. A laptop you also use at home is less clear. Then there’s the coffee you bought while editing, the outfit for a client presentation and the course that could help you win different work. 

Creative freelancing doesn’t always have a neat boundary between working life and personal life. That can make expenses confusing—and it’s one of the things we discuss in this wide-ranging article, as follows:

The basic test for expenses

For UK sole traders, an allowable expense is a qualifying business cost you deduct when calculating taxable profit. This article covers sole traders; limited companies have separate rules.  

The basic test is that a cost is incurred “wholly and exclusively” for your business. In plain English, it needs to be for your business rather than for you.  

Where you can identify a separate business share, such as part of a phone bill, you can claim that share.  

Where one purchase serves both purposes at once, such as an outfit you’d also wear socially, you generally can’t claim any of it. 

For the wider categories and claiming process, read our guide to allowable expenses for the self-employed. Here, we focus on the everyday decisions creative freelancers face: shared equipment, software, training and spending while you work.  

Understand what claiming an expense means 

Claiming an expense doesn’t mean HMRC refunds the purchase price. 

Suppose you receive £30,000 in business income and have £5,000 of allowable expenses. Your profit before other tax adjustments is £25,000.  

If all of that £5,000 would otherwise have been taxed at the basic rate of Income Tax (20%) and the main rate of Class 4 National Insurance (6%), claiming it reduces your bill by about £1,300. 

You’ve still spent £5,000, so those purchases cost you about £3,700 overall. Your own figures will depend on your circumstances.

 Tax relief reduces the cost without removing it, so a purchase needs to be worthwhile and affordable in its own right. 

Also check whether you’re using the £1,000 trading allowance. You cannot deduct actual expenses as well as claiming that allowance against the same income. 

Check common creative business costs 

Start with what you bought and how it supports your work. These categories give you a useful starting point, rather than automatic approval of every purchase within them. 

Cost

What to check

Design, writing or editing software 

Regular licence payments for business software can qualify. Exclude personal use. 

Fonts, stock images, music licences and plug-ins 

Licences for assets you use in client or business work can qualify. Exclude personal projects. 

Printing, stationery and postage 

Keep evidence of their business purpose. 

Laptop, camera or other equipment 

Treatment depends on your accounting method and business use. 

Studio or workspace rent 

Business premises costs can qualify; exclude private use. 

Portfolio website and advertising 

Business website and advertising costs can qualify. 

Professional membership or journals 

Check that they relate to your business. 

Training 

Must relate to your current business, including new skills it needs. 

These categories follow HMRC’s guidance on office costs, marketing, subscriptions, insurance, financial costs and training.  

Since the 2024–25 tax year, the cash basis has been the default accounting method for sole traders unless you opt out. 

HMRC’s office and equipment guidance distinguishes between cash basis and traditional accounting. Under cash basis, business equipment such as computers is generally claimed as an expense, although cars are treated differently.  

Under traditional accounting, equipment you keep for the business generally falls under capital allowances instead.  

For training, the rules extend beyond refreshing existing skills. Training can also support changes in your industry or develop skills needed to run your business, including administration. Courses to start a new business or enter an unrelated business area do not qualify under this guidance.  

Separate business and personal use 

Some purchases serve both purposes. Your phone might handle client calls and family messages. A laptop might hold paid projects and personal photos. 

Where business use can be separated, claim that share and keep a reasonable explanation of how you calculated it. 

For example, if an annual phone bill is £600 and a supportable calculation shows 40% business use, the business portion is £240. The percentage is illustrative, not a standard HMRC allowance. 

Working from home needs a calculation too. HMRC’s guidance allows a reasonable division of qualifying household costs, using factors such as rooms and time spent working. You may alternatively be eligible for simplified expenses.  

You cannot assume every mixed-purpose purchase can be divided. Ordinary clothing, for example, doesn’t become partly deductible because you wear it to client meetings, as it still serves a personal purpose.  

Paying from a business account also doesn’t settle the question. It records where the money came from, rather than proving the cost qualifies. 

Watch the costs that look claimable 

Don’t let the following items catch you out!

Coffee and food while you work 

In Money Diary of a sportswear entrepreneur, the owner takes her laptop to a café to work through emails and admin, recording spending on drinks and cakes.  

It’s a recognisable way to get work done. But buying refreshments while working doesn’t, by itself, make them allowable. 

Ordinary food and drink are generally personal living costs. Different rules can apply to qualifying business travel, including necessary overnight trips and certain occasional journeys. Check HMRC’s subsistence guidance before claiming.  

Client lunches and entertainment 

Discussing a project over lunch doesn’t usually make the hospitality deductible. HMRC generally excludes client entertaining, including food and drink provided during a work meeting. 

Costs of promoting your business, such as advertising or your website, are treated differently. 

Clothes for meetings or events 

Everyday clothing is not allowable, even when you buy it for work. That includes ordinary suits, shirts, dresses and shoes. 

Qualifying protective clothing, uniforms and costumes for actors or entertainers can be different. A smart outfit for a pitch isn’t automatically a uniform.  

Travel 

Genuine business travel may qualify, but private journeys and ordinary travel between home and work do not. 

Record the destination and purpose. If you regularly work at a client site or combine a trip with a holiday, check the treatment rather than assuming the whole journey qualifies. 

HMRC’s travel guide sets out the main categories and exclusions.  

Build a record you can explain 

Save the receipt or invoice as soon as you can, then add any context that won’t be obvious later: the project, business purpose and calculation of private use. 

A bank transaction may show you spent £85, but it won’t necessarily explain what you bought or why. 

At the Small and Medium-Sized Business (SMB) Advisory Board convened by Sage in September 2026, one sole trader described categorising transactions for Making Tax Digital as “a complete and utter minefield.”

That experience highlights a useful distinction. Choosing a category in your records and deciding whether a cost is allowable are separate questions. If you’re unsure about either, keep the receipt and a note explaining the purchase so you can check it. 

If you use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, your categorised records also feed your quarterly updates, so keeping them current saves a scramble later. 

A simple routine is enough to get started: 

Capture the receipt or invoice. 

Record the date, supplier and amount. 

Add the business purpose where needed. 

Separate private spending or mixed use. 

Flag uncertain items for checking. 

Keeping the evidence doesn’t necessarily mean building a pile of paper receipts. HMRC accepts records kept on paper or digitally, so a photo or scan of a receipt can do the job. 

HMRC requires accurate records and proof of expenses, although you don’t normally send the evidence with your tax return. Keep self-employed records for at least five years after the relevant 31 January submission deadline, subject to special rules for very late returns.  

If you’re unsure, retain the evidence and ask your accountant or HMRC a specific question. “Can I claim this course, which teaches a new tool used in my existing design business?” is more useful than “Can freelancers claim courses?” 

Final thoughts

Start with your last month of spending. Identify clear business costs, separate personal purchases and make a short list of items to check. That gives you a repeatable process for the next month too. 

FAQs about freelancer expenses 

			

			

	

Can I claim a laptop I also use personally? 

	

			

You may be able to claim the business share. Keep a reasonable calculation of usage. Under the cash basis, which applies to most sole traders, you’d usually claim that share as an expense. Under traditional accounting, it goes through capital allowances instead.  

	

	

Can I claim coffee when I work in a café? 

	

			

Working there doesn’t automatically make refreshments deductible. Ordinary food and drink are generally personal costs. Qualifying business travel can be different, so check the circumstances.  

	

	

Can I claim a course that teaches me something new? 

	

	

	

Do I need a business account to claim expenses? 

	

			

The account used doesn’t determine whether the cost qualifies. Separate accounts can make records easier to manage, but you still need evidence and a clear business purpose. 

	

	

Can I claim expenses and the trading allowance? 

	

			

You cannot claim actual expenses alongside the  trading allowance against the same income. If your allowable expenses come to less than £1,000 (£3,000 as of April 2027), the allowance usually gives you the bigger deduction. If they’re higher, claiming actual expenses usually does.

Key takeaways

Allowable expenses reduce taxable profit; they don’t make a purchase free.

title: What changes when small business owners get the numbers sooner?
snippet: Getting your financial information sooner gives you more time to act. Discover how Trinity Dental changed its processes, and what its experience could mean for your next business decision. The post What changes when small business owners get the numbers sooner? appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Key takeaways

Financial information, when it arrives in good time, gives small business owners more options before they need to act. 

Moving from paper-based administration to connected digital records can make useful financial information available sooner. 

Earlier information can give owners more time to prepare for liabilities and assess investment or hiring decisions. 

Sharing routine processing can reduce dependence on the owner while allowing them to retain oversight. 

Review one recent decision and ask whether earlier information would have changed your options. 

Accurate financial information can still arrive too late to help with a decision. Once a payment is due, an investment window has passed or a staffing decision has become urgent, the numbers may explain the situation without leaving you much room to change it. 

For Trinity Dental, delayed financial information left little time to prepare for tax bills or investment planning. Bringing that information forward gave the practice more opportunity to understand upcoming commitments and assess what it could afford to do next. 

The useful question is: do you know your numbers early enough to change your next decision? Trinity Dental Director Alison Simpson says: “I think instinct is important to have in a business, but it’s actually great to have the numbers to back it up.”

Here’s what we cover: 

When information arrives too late to plan 

See our video above to learn more about Trinity Dental, or read on for our analysis. 

Knowing about a liability shortly before payment is due leaves a different set of options from seeing it months ahead. More notice gives you time to consider that commitment alongside recruitment, equipment and other demands on cash. 

Trinity Dental wanted to invest in technology, people and the patient experience. The challenge was understanding when the business could make those commitments while also preparing for its tax bills. 

Earlier information cannot remove uncertainty or guarantee that an investment will work. It can give you time to examine the assumptions, discuss the options with your accountant and make a decision before it becomes urgent. 

Alison says: “In the past, I would have been given a tax bill from the accountant and then have to find that money. Whereas now, we’re ready for it.” 

What changed in the financial process 

The practice’s earlier approach relied heavily on paper invoices and statements. Documents had to be found, spread out, matched manually and filed. Keeping the records up to date involved working through that accumulated paperwork. 

Trinity Dental introduced Sage to bring documents and accounting information into a digital process. The team could scan documents and handle smaller amounts of processing more regularly, while cloud access made records available without having to find the physical paperwork. 

Adelaine Ginns, Operations Lead at Trinity Dental, took on more of the regular financial processing, while Alison Simpson retained oversight through reports and discussions with the practice’s accountant. The change involved both a different way of handling information and a clearer division of the work. 

Adelaine says: “When we were doing the paper version of the invoicing, it would take us up to two full days, and now with Sage, it takes us a couple of hours.” 

Using financial information to assess a hire 

At Trinity Dental, missed-call data helped Alison identify a need for more reception capacity. She then used the practice’s financial information to assess whether another team member’s salary would fit within her staffing-cost benchmark. “So I knew then that Trinity could definitely allow that change and allow it comfortably,” Alison explains. 

The operational information showed where extra capacity was needed. The financial information helped establish whether the practice could afford it. Together, they gave Alison a clearer basis for assessing the hire. 

The same approach applies to an equipment purchase or another investment. Establish the business need, then use the financial information to test the timing and affordability. 

Sharing work without giving up oversight 

Receiving figures earlier creates more time to plan. Redesigning the process and assigning routine work differently can also reduce the amount of administration that depends on the owner. 

Trinity Dental’s division of responsibilities illustrates an important distinction: processing and oversight do not have to be the same job. An owner can review the financial picture and work with their accountant without personally completing every routine step. 

If you want to share more of the work, start by making responsibilities clear. Who processes the documents? Who checks that the information is complete? Which questions need to come back to you or your accountant? Access to software helps, but the process also needs to be understandable to the people using it. 

Alison says: “You can bring on the best technology available, but if you don’t have the right people to actually make those changes, then the technology is just not going to be successful.” 

Check the timing of one real decision 

Choose one recent decision: a hire, a purchase, an investment or a payment that required preparation. Write down when you needed to decide and when you received the financial information to assess it. How much time did that leave to consider your options? 

If the information arrived too late to influence the outcome, work backwards. Was paperwork accumulating? Were transactions processed infrequently? Did information sit with one person? Or did reports become available only after the decision was needed? 

The answer helps identify what to change. You might need more regular processing, clearer responsibilities, better access to records or an earlier conversation with your accountant. Start with the delay that affected the decision, then work out which improvement would address it. 

Final thoughts: More notice to make your next decision 

Trinity Dental’s experience connects the everyday work of processing financial records with the bigger question of how a small business owner plans ahead. More current information is useful when it helps your business prepare for commitments and assess its next investment. 

For your own business, start with one upcoming decision. Work out what you need to know, who can provide it and when you need it. That gives you a practical test of whether your financial process is delivering accurate information in time to use it. 

FAQs

			

			

	

How can I tell if my financial information is arriving too late? 

	

			

Compare when you received the information for a recent decision with when you needed to act. If there was little time to assess your options, review what delayed the information and whether it could have been available sooner. 

	

	

Which business decisions benefit from earlier financial information? 

	

			

Decisions about investment, equipment and recruitment, as well as preparing for upcoming liabilities, can benefit. Earlier information gives you more time to assess a commitment alongside other demands on the business. 

	

	

Does faster financial reporting automatically reduce your workload? 

	

			

No. Earlier reporting can give you more time to plan, but reducing your workload may require changes to how routine work is completed and who is responsible for it. 

	

	

How can financial work be shared without you losing oversight? 

	

			

Give routine processing a clear owner and agree how it will be checked. You can then review reports, monitor commitments and discuss decisions with the accountant without completing every processing task. 

	

	

What should a business review before changing its accounting process? 

	

			

Look at how documents are collected, how often transactions are processed, who can access the information, and when reports become available. Connect that review to a decision where the business needed better or earlier information.
